svg.text: Access Control — the 4 planes (one coherent model)
"Access control" is NOT one thing. Four planes, different mechanisms. Blurring them is the junior mistake; a bank cares most about planes 3 & 4 and the "what about—" follow-ups (orange).
The thread through all four: least privilege · deny by default · short-lived credentials · every grant is attested + auditable · no long-lived stored secrets anywhere.
Identity is the new perimeter — you don't trust the network, you verify identity on every access, human or machine. Every access DECISION is itself an audit event (→ immutable log).
End-user access
customer / admin → the application
Question: "who is this user, what may they do?"
Authentication (who you are)
• Entra External ID / CIAM for customers
• OAuth2 / OIDC — token-based, standards
• MFA · Conditional Access (device, risk,
named location)
• session mgmt: short tokens + refresh
Authorization (what you may do)
• RBAC — role → permissions (coarse)
• ABAC — attributes (dept, amount, region)
for fine-grained + contextual rules
• enforced at the API Gateway (Apigee)
BEFORE the request hits a service
Enforcement lives in two layers
Gateway = token + coarse scope (valid, authorized caller?). Service = fine-grained (can THIS
user touch THIS record?). "Coarse authz at the gateway, fine-grained in the service — never
rely on the edge alone."
◆ Follow-up: how do you REVOKE immediately?
A JWT is valid until it expires — a fired employee's token keeps working. Answer: very short
token TTL (minutes) to shrink the window + a deny-list / introspection endpoint for instant kill + refresh-token rotation.
◆ Follow-up: authz at the DATA layer (defense in depth)
Row-Level Security + column masking in the DB itself, so even if service logic has a bug the
database won't return rows/columns the user shouldn't see. Belt and braces on fine-grained authz.
Service-to-service access
one microservice → another (east-west)
Question: "is this really claim-svc calling, or an impostor?"
mTLS via the service mesh (Istio)
• every service presents a cert; BOTH sides verify — mutual, not one-way TLS
• identity = a SPIFFE ID in an X.509 SVID (spiffe://bank/ns/prod/sa/payment)
• sidecar handles issue + rotation — zero TLS code in the app
• SPIRE issues SVIDs by ATTESTATION, short-lived + auto-rotated
Default-deny east-west
NetworkPolicy + mesh authz policy: a service can ONLY call the services it's allowed to.
A breached pod can't freely pivot — only its allowlisted neighbours.
For a bank, east-west encryption is a stated control, not just good practice. Say that.
Zero-trust: verify identity on every internal call, not just at the edge.
◆ Follow-up: secrets rotation & the "secret zero" problem
For the few secrets that MUST exist (3rd-party API keys): Key Vault with automated rotation
on a schedule, versioned, fetched at runtime.
"Secret zero" = how does the pod auth to Key Vault in the FIRST place? Answer: it doesn't hold
a secret — workload identity (plane 4) bootstraps it. That's the loop closed: no secret to fetch
the secrets. The chain terminates in platform-attested identity, not a planted credential.
Human operator → infrastructure
engineers accessing cluster / cloud — BFSI differentiator
Question: "how does a human get admin, and can we prove who did what?"
Just-in-time, not standing access
• PIM — request elevation, time-boxed,
approval required, MFA on activation
• nobody holds standing admin — you
elevate for 2h, then it drops
• every activation logged →
the audit trail auditors ask for
The controls a bank audit checks
• break-glass: 2 accounts, excluded from
CA, hardware MFA, alert on ANY use
• access reviews — periodic recertify
• Bastion / no public SSH-RDP; JIT VM
• segregation of duties (approver ≠
requester)
◆ Follow-up: who can read production DATA? (the sharpest audit question)
Infra-admin ≠ data-access. A DBA reading prod customer records is a higher-sensitivity grant:
JIT-elevated too, every query audited, dynamic data masking so even privileged queries see
masked PII unless explicitly authorized. "Access to the box is not access to the data."
Why this plane is the BFSI differentiator
Most candidates answer "access control" with plane 1 and stop. Audit findings land HERE —
standing admin, shared accounts, no MFA on elevation, no review trail, unaudited data access.
Naming PIM + break-glass + access reviews + data-access auditing unprompted marks you as
someone who's been through a real security review, not just built a login page.
Line: "no standing privilege — access is requested, time-boxed, approved, and logged."
And: "access to the infrastructure is a separate, lower grant than access to the data."
Workload → resource (DB / secret)
a pod reaching a database or Key Vault — BFSI differentiator
Question: "how does a pod auth to a DB WITHOUT a stored password?"
Workload identity — no static secrets
• pod's identity (K8s service account) federates to cloud IAM →
gets a SHORT-LIVED token for the DB / Key Vault. Nothing stored, nothing to leak.
• Azure: Managed / Workload Identity · AWS: IRSA · GCP: Workload Identity
• cross-cloud: Workload Identity Federation (the GKE→Entra ID case)
• secrets that must exist → Key Vault, runtime fetch, never in the image
Why "no stored secret" is the whole game
A password in a config / env var / image layer is the #1 way credentials leak — committed to
git, logged, or copied. Workload identity removes the secret: platform attests the pod and
issues a token that expires in minutes.
Same principle as plane 2 (SPIFFE) and plane 3 (PIM): identity is EARNED + short-lived,
never a long-lived secret you hold.
◆ Ties to your audit design: every access DECISION is an audit event
Who authenticated, whose token was issued, which human elevated via PIM, which pod got a DB
token, which DBA ran which query — all flow to the SAME immutable WORM audit log from the
observability design. Access control produces the evidence; the audit pipeline stores it tamper-proof.
"Every grant is logged to the immutable audit trail — access control and audit are one story,
not two. A grant you can't prove happened is a grant you can't defend in an audit."
How to walk it — the coherent model
Open by splitting it — the seniority move.
"Access control is four planes: end-user, service-to-service, human-operator-to-infrastructure, and workload-to-resource. Different mechanisms each, and
for a bank the last two matter most — privileged human access and secretless workload access are where audit findings actually land."
1 End-user:
OIDC/OAuth2 + MFA/Conditional Access; RBAC coarse + ABAC contextual. Coarse authz at gateway, fine-grained in service, and Row-Level Security in the
DB as defense in depth. Revocation: short token TTL + a deny-list/introspection endpoint for instant kill — a JWT is otherwise valid till it expires.
2 Service-to-service:
mTLS in the mesh, SPIFFE identity in an SVID, sidecar-rotated, default-deny east-west. Secrets that must exist: Key Vault with auto-rotation, and the
secret-zero problem is solved by workload identity — the pod doesn't hold a secret to fetch the secrets.
3 Human operator (differentiator):
No standing admin — PIM just-in-time, time-boxed, approved, MFA'd, logged. Break-glass monitored, access reviews, Bastion, segregation of duties. And
the sharp one: access to the DATA is a separate, higher grant than access to the box — DBA queries are JIT, audited, and see masked PII by default.
4 Workload-to-resource (differentiator):
Workload identity — pod federates to cloud IAM for a short-lived DB/Key Vault token, nothing stored. Managed Identity / IRSA / Workload Identity;
federation across clouds. Secrets that must exist live in Key Vault, auto-rotated, runtime-fetched, never in the image.
The one thread that unifies all four:
Every plane replaces a long-lived stored credential with a short-lived ATTESTED identity. User tokens refresh, service SVIDs rotate, human admin is JIT
via PIM, pod DB access is a minutes-long federated token. "Identity is earned and short-lived, never a secret you hold." And every grant lands in the
immutable audit log — access control and audit are one story. That's zero-trust applied consistently to humans and machines alike.
One-paragraph answer:
"Four planes. End users: OIDC + MFA, RBAC/ABAC, coarse authz at the gateway, fine-grained in the service, RLS in the DB; short token TTL plus a
deny-list for instant revocation. Services: mTLS with SPIFFE identity, default-deny east-west. Human operators: no standing admin — PIM just-in-time,
break-glass, access reviews, and data access audited separately from infra access. Workloads: identity federation for short-lived DB/secret tokens,
nothing stored. The thread is short-lived attested identity over long-lived secrets, every grant logged to the immutable trail — zero-trust for humans and
machines the same way."
